translations.text:
A for Allah who has my heart,
I have no knowledge of B,
nor do I know what it means,
while A savours sweet to me.
I can't tell between O and Q,
it makes me dither and delve;
Bulleh, look after the first,
the rest will take care of itself.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.35. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training. Rafat maps the Urdu letters ain/ghain to English O/Q, so this is a literary adaptation._

Alif — Allah — has dyed my heart;
of "be" I have no knowledge at all.
Reading "be", nothing comes clear to me,
while the sweetness of Alif has arrived.
I know no difference between ain and ghain —
this alone has Alif taught me.
Bulleh, hold fast the words of Alif
that scour the heart clean.

translations.text:
The last stars have been scrubbed from the skies.
Wayfarer, arise!
    The camp is astir, you are too slow,
    your companions are ready to go.
    Are you deaf to the clangour and cries?
Wayfarer, arise!
    Up, up, from too much fuss refrain,
    for you will not come this way again;
    the rest are saddled up, unwise.
Wayfarer, arise!
    You check each article you own
    when none will help. So much to be done
    and you laze in bed with tight-shut eyes.
Wayfarer, arise!

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.39. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

Now wake, beloved traveller —
the night has passed, the stars have all sunk low.
Come, the resting-houses stand open;
your fellow-travellers are ready, waiting on you.
Do you still not hear the drums resound?
Now wake, beloved traveller.
The turning wheel of days has come round;
there will be no returning, no coming back for you.
Your companions cry, "Move on, move on!"
Now wake, beloved traveller.
Pearls, silver, the philosopher's stone lie near you,
the ocean is beside you — yet you die of thirst.
Open your eyes, rise — the door stands idle.
Now wake, beloved traveller.

Where is your home?
Whence did you come?
Where do you go?

The place you pride in
will go for a song;
kill, rob the poor,
think yourself strong;
your four days reign
will end before long;
you will soon be put
where you belong.

The Boatman's ferry is full
each time it crosses.
Bulleh, you old sinner,
reckon your losses.

Where is your home?
Whence did you come?
Where do you go?

Name your dwelling — where did you come from, where must you go?
The station you take pride in
will not go along with you.
You do violence and torment people;
you have made plunder your trade.
After a few days' merriment
in the end you must rise and go.
Come, let us dwell in the City of the Silent,
where whole kingdoms lie contained.
Boatload after boatload the mighty ferryman carries across —
Azrael, the Angel of Death, the boatman.
Of all of these, Bulleh,
he is the oldest sinner.
Name your dwelling — where did you come from, where must you go?

Embrace me, love, and hold me next your heart.
What sinister jungles stand in my way,
what snakes, what beasts of prey,

One glimpse of you and I shall be at peace.

Merge me into Yourself, beloved! Merge me into Yourself.
The roads are beset with raiders, comrade — jungle, thicket, terrors;

on the far side of You the ground rears up, with a hundred thousand thorns and dangers.
With dread the heart trembles and shakes — ferry my boat across.
Show Bulleh Shah the Beloved's face; lift the veil and reveal it.
Merge me into Yourself, beloved! Merge me into Yourself.

God, what shall I do?
        Nothing can induce them to stay;
        rather, they propagate despair.

        and goodbyes echo in the air.
                God, what shall I do?

        I see them everywhere.
                God, what shall I do?

The friends next door have risen and gone —

They have risen and gone, they stay no longer;

O Lord, what shall we do now!

on every side a cry has risen.
O Lord, what shall we do now!
The heart, searching, blazes up in flame
without beholding the Beloved's sight.
O Lord, what shall we do now!
Bulleh! without the dear Lord
there is neither this shore nor the far.

translations.text:
I will use a spell
to get my lost love back.
        And breathe this spell on the air,
        the sun will make it warm.
        Black are my eyes and eyebrows,
        they will brew up a storm.
        I have an ocean within me
        whose tides none can becalm.
        Although I am a virgin
        there's a babe on my arm.

        Like the lightning I will flash
        and thunder like the cloud.
        I crackle in love's flames,
        the moon will weave me a shroud.

        I shall roam like a gipsy
        and sing my plaint aloud,
        till the sap of my passion
        runs madly through each clod.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), pp.55, 57 (the poem runs across two spreads). COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

I will sing a spell of my own;
I will win back my estranged love.
This spell I will recite and blow;
I will set the sun's fire ablaze.
Kohl in my eyes, dark clouds —
from my brows I will summon a storm.
Seven seas within the heart —
from the heart I will raise a wave.
Neither wife am I nor maiden,
yet I will dandle a son in my lap.
Turning to lightning I will flash and terrify;
turning to cloud I will thunder.
Love is my brazier, wild rue smoulders;
from the moon I will make a shroud.
Upon the seat of the Placeless
I will sit and sound the mystic note.
I will clasp my Lord to my breast,
and then be called His woman.

translations.text:
One is enough.  Break the counting-frames,
forget hell's terrors and its flames,
purify your dreams and desires,
belief and unbelief are just names.

    Truth stands in the hall.
    One point settles it all.

In prayer why abrade your forehead?
Away with it, tear down the facade
of morality.  Causing people pain
is the only sin you should dread.

    The writing is on the wall.
    One point settles it all.

To the same jungle the hawks repair
and seed by seed they scrounge there;
in this their energy is spent,
and they are left gasping for air.

    Prayer is body's gall.
    One point settles it all.

From a pilgrimage some have returned,
but any merit they may have earned,
despite humility in dress,
in percentage and shady deals is burned.

    Truth stands too tall.
    One point settles it all.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), pp.61+63. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training. Rafat renders the refrain freely (each stanza's first refrain-line varies while "One point settles it all" recurs) and adapts the imagery._

In one point the whole matter is closed.

Seize the point, let go of your reckonings;
give up dread of hell and the grave's torments.
Bolt shut the doors of unbelief,
scour clean the dreamings of the heart —
the matter comes home to such a house:
in one point the whole matter is closed.

For nothing you grind your brow on the ground,
prostrate long to show off at the prayer-niche,
recite the creed to make people gape,
yet plant no understanding inside the heart.
Even the true word one day runs out:
in one point the whole matter is closed.

Off to a forest the [birds] fly,
living on a single grain a day;
the mindless only wear their bodies out
and drag themselves home spent.
[The soul frets deep within]:
in one point the whole matter is closed.

Many come back turned into pilgrims,
draping blue robes about themselves,
strutting and swaying through the Hajj —
but whom does such a show please?
Somewhere even the true word is stopped:
in one point the whole matter is closed.

translations.text:
In a topsy-turvy world I saw the truth unroll

Crows peck at scarecrows, pigeons fell the hawk,
and asses have assumed the horse's role.

Nor aunt nor uncle now receives respect;
children shun the path where parents stroll.

The old on bare boards sit while newness struts,
liars have mansions, truth has the begging-bowl.

It was so ordained, Bulleh, accept the fact,
on carpets graced by lords the lackeys loll.

In a topsy-turvy world I saw the truth unroll.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.65. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training. Rafat compresses the animal-reversal imagery and re-orders couplets freely._

Topsy-turvy times have come — so I have set my verse to the beat.

Crows have fallen to striking the eagles, and sparrows have toppled the towers;
horses are left to peck at gravel, while donkeys are bought at a price.

Among one's own there is no affection — what of uncles now, what of aunts;
no concord of father with sons, nor of mothers with their daughters.

The truthful meet with nothing but shoves, the liar is seated in the place of honour;
those once foremost sit destitute, while the hindmost spread out their carpets.

Men of the hovels are crowned as kings, and kings are sent out to beg.
Bulleh, the command has come from the Presence — who is there to turn it aside?

Topsy-turvy times have come — so I have set my verse to the beat.

translations.text:
I welcome those who come, bless those who depart,
but not for a moment can I bear to part
from my love. I dream of love, and wake to love,
or scare the crows from my embattled heart.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.67. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

Alif — I am a sacrifice to those who come, and give myself up for those who go.
A fine love has caught fast in my eye; not for an hour, not a single moment, have I let the Friend slip from mind.
My very bones waste away in longing; I sit shooing the crow off, watching for a sign of him.
Bulleh, I have gone mad for the Beloved — I keep calling out to the Friend, that he may hear.

translations.text:
Who am I?  Does anyone know?

In a mosque no worshipper,
nor a temple-frequenter,
I'm not pure, nor impure,
nor Moses, nor Pharaoh.

    Does anyone know?

What is good, what badness?
What is mirth, what sadness?
I'm not earth, water, fire,
nor the winds that blow.

    Does anyone know?

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.69. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training. Rafat renders the refrain "Bulleh, ki jaana main kaun" as "Does anyone know?" and reworks the second stanza's imagery._

Bulleh — what do I know of who I am?

I am no believer in the mosque,
nor do I keep the rites of unbelief;
I am neither pure among the pure, nor defiled;
I am not Moses, and not Pharaoh.
Bulleh — what do I know of who I am?

I am neither impurity nor purity,
neither the joy of a wedding nor grief;
I am not of water, and not of earth,
not of fire, and not of wind.
Bulleh — what do I know of who I am?

Every female from near and afar
turned up to brief Bulleh Shah.
Listen Bulleh, they said, it's a sin
to condemn the prophet's kin.
Those who acknowledge them, you tell,
will get the one-way ticket to hell.
Does sanctity deserve such scorn?

It's God's carelessness where one is born.
When I put the pretty ones in their place
the ugly shoved their noses in my face.
If you seek redemption drop this farce.
My caste?  I've none.  I'm just a man.

They came to counsel Bulleh — the sisters and the sisters-in-law:

"Take our advice, Bulleh — let go the Arain's hem!
You, of the Prophet's house, of Ali's line — why have you brought this stain on us?"

Whoever calls me a Sayyid — may the torments of hell be his;
whoever calls me a Rai (Arain) — the swings of paradise are his.

He pushes the lovely ones aside and clasps the homely to His breast.

If you long for the garden in bloom, become a servant of the Arain.
Why ask what caste Bulleh Shah is? Be content within His will.

title: Patiyaan likhaan main shaam nu (Accursed)

original.text:
پتیاں لِکھاں میں شام نوں

پتیاں لِکھاں میں شام نوں، مینوں پیا نظر نہ آوے
آنگن بھانا ڈراوَنا، کِت بدھ رَین وِہاوے

پاندھے پنڈت جگت کے، میں پُچھ رہی آس لائے
پوتھی وید، کیا دوس ہے، جو اُلٹے بھاگ ہمارے

بھائیا وے جوتشیا! اِک سچی بات بھی کہیو
جے میں ہیٹی بھاگ دی، تم چُپ نہ رہیو

بھج سکاں تے بھج جاواں، سب چھڈ کے کراں فقیری
پر ڈولڑی ہے گل وچ پریم زنجیری

نیند گئی کِت دیس نوں، اوہ بھی وَیران میری
مت سُفنے میں آن مِلے، اوہ نیندر کیہڑی

رو رو جیو وِلاندیاں، غم کرنی آں دُونا
نیناں زہر بھی نہ چلن، کِسے کِیتا لُونا

ساجن تُمری پریت سے، مجھ کو ہاتھ کیہ آیا
چھتر سُولاں سِر جھالیا، پر تیرا پنتھ نہ پایا

پریم نگر چل ودیئے، جِتّے وَسّے کنت ہمارا
بُلھیا! شوہ توں منگنی ہاں، دے دے مینوں نظارا

translations.text:
He has not come. In the evening I sit
and write letters. The darkness scares me.
I ask each passing magus, why is it
everything I do turns out badly?

Astrologer, be kind, tell the truth
for once. Am I cursed? Was I born ill-fated?
If I could run away, I would, my youth
to beggary give, but with chains I'm weighted.

And even sleep has migrated, that he
may not enter my dreams. His absence sears
my heart. Someone has cast a spell on me
so that my eyes cannot even shed tears.

What was it I gained by love? Tantrum
after tantrum, and nothing but pain.
Yet all I wish for is to be near him,
to glimpse his beloved face once again.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.77. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training. (Book prints the title "ACCURSED"; the Contents lists it as "Accused.")_

I write letters in the evening, yet my beloved is nowhere in sight.
The empty courtyard frightens me — how am I to pass this night?

The wayfarers, the pandits of the world — I keep asking them in hope,
and the books, the Vedas: what is my fault, that my fortune runs reversed?

O brother astrologer! speak for once a single true word —
if I was born to a mean fate, then do not keep silent.

Could I flee, I would flee — give up everything and take to beggary —
but around my neck is wound the chain of love.

To what country has my sleep gone? — it too has forsaken me,
lest he come and meet me in dreams; and what sleep would that even be?

Weeping and wailing I drag out my life, doubling my own grief;
not even tears will run from my eyes — someone has cast a spell on me.

Beloved, from loving you, what did I ever gain in hand?
A canopy of thorns I bore upon my head, yet never found your path.

Let us go and dwell in the city of love, where my Beloved abides.
Bulleh, I beg only this of the Beloved: grant me one glimpse of your face.

original.text:
تیرے عشق نچائیاں

تیرے عشق نے ڈیرا میرے اندر کیتا
بھر کے زہر پیالہ میں تاں آپے پیتا
جھب سے بوہڑیں وے طبیبا، نہیں تے میں مر گیّا
تیرے عشق نچائیاں کر کے تھیّا تھیّا!

چھپ گیا وے سورج، باہر رہ گئی آ لالی
وے میں صدقے ہوواں، دیویں مُڑ جے وِکھالی
پیرا! میں بُھل گیّاں تیرے، نال نہ گیّا
تیرے عشق نچائیاں کر کے تھیّا تھیّا!

translations.text:
What a dance your love has led me

    since within me it opened its shop
    and I drank from its poisoned cup.
    Come to my help, apothecary.
        What a dance your love has led me!

    The sun has set; some redness remains.
    Unveil your face but once again
    to the simpleton who set you free.
        What a dance your love has led me!

    I would not be denied. Now the boat
    is in the whirlpool, barely afloat.
    I chose to stay on, foolishly.
        What a dance your love has led me!

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.79. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training. Rafat renders "ḍera keeta" as "opened its shop" and the third stanza's boat/boatmen imagery freely._

Your love has set me dancing — thaiyya, thaiyya!

Your love has pitched its camp inside me;
I filled the cup with poison and drank it down myself.
Come quickly to my side, O healer, or else I die.
Your love has set me dancing — thaiyya, thaiyya!

The sun has gone down; only a redness lingers in the sky.
I would give myself for you — if only you would turn and show your face once more.
O Master, I lost my way; I could not keep pace with you.
Your love has set me dancing — thaiyya, thaiyya!

Do not hold me back from this love, O mother —
the boat is going under; who now can turn it back?
My reason, gone astray, has drifted off with the boatmen.
Your love has set me dancing — thaiyya, thaiyya!

I'm in a trap.

Love brought me to this fate;
just one glimpse was the bait.
Did my zeal deserve this blow?

I'm in a trap.

Take pity on my innocence
and give me some recompense.
This death is much too slow.

I'm in a trap.

Within touching distance yet
I cannot reach your heart.
Love me, or let me go.

I'm in a trap.

My life is brought to the brink of ruin.

Your love weighs on me heavier than a mountain;
for the sake of one moment's glimpse it has plundered me whole.
Will my labour be requited, or not — this acquaintance with the Mighty One?
My life is brought to the brink of ruin.

The pure have only this one recourse: that You come running to me yourself.
When I wake, wake beside me; when I sleep, sleep alongside me.
Whoever set her heart on You — what ease did she ever gain?
My life is brought to the brink of ruin.

Your name shines through the world — why then do You flee the lover?
You suspend even love's own custom; You will not tell me Your secret.
[uncertain line — torn apart in the middle, left hanging upside down].
My life is brought to the brink of ruin.

translations.text:
Whatever you touch takes on your hue.

Your eyes have caused a stir, unveil yourself
like the cloud-swept moon when it breaks through.

This dumbness is not a pose. For those who die
before death can strike them, their life renew.

Too many obstacles! Now take my hand
and help me over them as if I flew.

Dance, Bulleh, dance, your love has come to you.
Whatever you touch takes on your hue.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.85. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training. Rafat renders the "die before you die" hadith and the immanence couplet freely._

Whatever hue was dyed, it was dyed deep and fast — the crimson of the murshid, O friend.

The pearl of meaning has raised a great clamour; lift the veil from your eyes, O friend.
In your black tresses be the radiant hand of Moses — show me that flash of light, O friend.

[Silence itself has become the highest silence]; keep faith with those who gave themselves to you, O friend.
"Die before you die" — then breathe life once more into the one who has died, O friend.

The quarrel of love is half-hidden; set your feet down with care, O friend.
You are Yourself within every thing; unveil Yourself and let Yourself be seen, O friend.

Bulleh — the Beloved has come to my house; dance and dance and show it, O friend!
Whatever hue was dyed, it was dyed deep and fast — the crimson of the murshid, O friend.

translations.text:
Be silent now.

To the others truth is phlegm,
when you pass they raise their hem,
it brings out the beast in them,
for they would rather not know.

Truth wrecks the dogmatist's pride,
it gives the lover a bride
and a gay new world beside,
and says to the pilgrim, go.

But how can the lover be spare
of words, when he looks at her hair
and smells that scent-drenched air?
Renounce, renounce, take the vow.

Be silent now.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.87. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training. Rafat keeps the aa/aa/aa/o rhyme-shape but words each "Sach…" line freely._

Let us pass our days keeping silent.

Hearing the truth, people will not sit still;
say the truth, and they fly at your throat;
they will not even sit beside the truthful —
yet to the loving lover, truth is sweet.

Truth brings the ruin of dogmatic law,
truth is a wedding in the lover's house,
truth raises a whole new settlement —
as befits one who has traded the Law for the Path.

The lover cannot keep his silence;
the one to whom truth has come is bound by it,
[bound by the fragrant knot of the Beloved's bridal joy] —
leave the world and its tangled spread behind.
Let us pass our days keeping silent.

translations.text:
Who's keeping the gossips busy?
What ecstatic being is here
who is so drenched in oneness
for caste he has no care?
    Whose fame has caused such a din,
    who is nearer than your skin,
    who says I reside within,
    here, there, everywhere?
Shun the ground where untruths hiss,
receive love's hallowed kiss,
be where your beloved is,
and nothing else will matter.

    None owns these heaps of rubble,
    life is nothing but trouble,
    wayfarer, learn to ride double
    with one giving care for care.
Bulleh Shah, take a cue,
whom you seek is seeking you,
blessings on all you do
if you surrender to His care.

Come, let us go and see that ecstatic one —
the one the spinning-circles are all abuzz about.
He is steeped in the dye of Oneness;
he never asks, "what caste are you, who are you?"
He whose clamour has spread on every side,
who dwells forever close beside you,
who says, "We are nearer" (naḥnu aqrab),
who says, "within your very selves" (fī anfusikum).
Leave behind the town of falsehood and illusion,
make firm within you the intoxication of love —
they have already reached the town of Truth.

It is neither yours nor mine —
this mortal world, a mere quarrel and squabble;
without a murshid, who can be the guide?
Recite: "Remember Me, and I will remember you" (fazkurūnī azkurkum).
Bulleh Shah, the whole thing turns on a subtle sign:
those seized by the longing for the Vision —
to them the trader-wayfarer's destination came in sight.
"The Hand of God is above their hands" (yadu-Llāhi fawqa aydīhim).

title: Khalq tamaashe aai yaar (The World's a Fun-fair)

خَلق تماشے آئی یار

اَج کیہ کیتا؛ کل کیہ کرنا؛ وَت اساڈا آیا!
اَیسی واہ کِیاری بیجی، چڑیاں کھیت وَنجایا

translations.text:
The world's a fun-fair.

What did I do today? What of tomorrow?
A bad ploughing will only bring sorrow.

The world and my love made me their slave.
But you'll go empty-handed to the grave.

Each in his turn youngster and old man fade,
innkeeper and servingman, mistress and maid.

To win his love, Bulleh exercises his wits;
first fashions a pot, then shatters it to bits.

Stroll through the bazar, join the revelry there,
then on to the next. The world's a fun-fair.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.95. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training. Rafat renders the refrain "khalq tamaashe aai" as "The world's a fun-fair" and re-orders/compresses the imagery._

The people have come out to the spectacle, O friend!

What did I do today? What must I do tomorrow? — and now our turn has come round!
Such was the plot I sowed that the birds laid the whole field to waste.

One reproach comes from the loved ones, the other from the world;
the honour and shame of this place stay here — one lets go and clutches at the dust, O friend.

He makes one young, He makes one old — each gets his own turn:
be it noblewoman or bondmaid or slave-girl, be it washerwoman or innkeeper's wife.

Bulleh sets out to see the Beloved, and makes of himself a pretext;
having shaped all manner of pots, He breaks them back into shards.

Watch this show and pass along; go and look at the next bazaar;
what a throng has gathered at the court — the people have come out to the spectacle, O friend!

and some are sadly walking.

My heart longs for the beloved Maahi.

Some, laughing and laughing, chatter away;
others wander about weeping and searching.
Tell the spring in all its blossoming —
my heart longs for the beloved Maahi.

I was left all bathed and adorned, still waiting;
some knot has turned the Beloved's heart away.
Let me set fire to all my finery —
my heart longs for the beloved Maahi.

The tale-bearers have left me wounded;
torments have ringed me round on every side.
Come home, Maahi — grant me one sight of you —
my heart longs for the beloved Maahi.

تیکلے توں وَل پَئے جاندے، کون لُہار سدا وے
تیکلے توں وَل لاہیں لُہارا، تَندی ٹُٹ ٹُٹ جاوے
گُھمڑی گھُمڑی ایہ جھوٹے کھاندا، چھَٹّی اِک نہ لاہوے
پِیّا نہیں جو بیڑی بَنّھاں، بائٹ ہتھ نہ آوے
چمڑیاں لُتّے چوپڑ ناہیں، ماہل پَئی بَڑلاوے

جِت وَل یار اُتّے وَل اکھیاں، دِل میرا بیلے دھاوے
ترنجن کِتّن سَدن سہیلیاں، برہوں ڈھول وجاوے
عرض ایہو، مینوں آن مِلے ہُن، کون وسیلہ جاوے
سُتّے مَناں دا کَت لیا اُٹھّا، مینوں شوہ گَل لاوے

translations.text:
The spinning-wheel is broken,
        I cannot spin.
Call the smith, for the axle
        wobbles on its pin.
The thread keeps breaking, smith,
        Let your job be neat;
it sways so that not a spool
        comes off complete.
I cannot tie it well, it slips
        again and again;
its grease is all used up,
        it creaks and groans.
The spinning-wheel is broken,
        I cannot spin.

How shall this long day pass
        till I can meet
my love? He is gone with the cows
        and my mind's feet
follow him to the pasture.
        The girls say come
and spin, but my heart is heavy,
        and hands numb.
Come back, love, come back again,
        my heart makes din,
reach out your arms to me
        and take me in.
The spinning-wheel is broken,
        I cannot spin.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.99. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training. Rafat breaks each Punjabi line into an indented two-part unit and words the mechanism-imagery freely._

The spinning-wheel's handle has slipped — no spinning can be done at all.
The spindle keeps bending out of true — who will go and call the smith?
Straighten the bent spindle, O smith — the thread keeps snapping, snapping;
round and round it wobbles and jerks, and not one full spool winds off.
Whatever thread I wind will not hold; nothing comes right to hand;
the leather straps are dry of grease, the drive-belt whines and groans.
The spinning-wheel's handle has slipped — no spinning can be done at all.

How is this endless day to pass? — may my darling show me his face.
Maahi has gone off with the buffaloes; who has any heart to spin?
Wherever the Friend turns, there turn my eyes; my heart races to the pasture.
The spinning-companions call me to the wheel, but separation beats its drum.
This alone is my plea: let him come to me now — what go-between shall I send?
[the reckoning of my sleeping heart is settled] — let the Beloved fold me to his breast.
How is this endless day to pass? — may my darling show me his face.

translations.text:
'Ranjha, Ranjha' I cried till only Ranjha is there?
I'm transformed, now Heer has disappeared.

We are synonymous: one heart, a single thought,
I am expunged, and Ranjha stands out clear.

Since he is inside me, he is all that exists,
that which I show to the world is just veneer.

Don the sackcloth, throw the white dress away,
for they are covered with stains who whiteness wear.

Hazara calls me, in Sial no friends are near.
'Ranjha, Ranjha' I cried till only Ranjha is here.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.101. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training. (Scan contains typos: "Ranhja", "trarnsformed".)_

Crying out "Ranjha, Ranjha," I have myself now become Ranjha.
Call me Dhido-Ranjha now; let no one call me "Heer."

Ranjha is within me, and I within Ranjha — no other thought remains;
I am not: it is He alone, consoling His own self.

Whatever dwells within us, that is our very essence;
the one I gave my love to — I have become just like him.

Cast off the white sheet, girl, and put on the faqir's coarse blanket;
the white sheet will show every stain, but the blanket takes no stain.

Take me to Takht Hazara, Bulleh — among the Sials I find no refuge.
Crying out "Ranjha, Ranjha," I have myself now become Ranjha.

Fasting, pilgrimage, and the call
to prayer, love has drowned them all.
    Can any artifice survive
    when messages of love arrive?
    On the ears only its sounds fall.
        Fasting, pilgrimage, and the call
        to prayer, love has drowned them all.

The moment Love came toward
me, rituals went by the board.
Love, only love, was then to be seen,
over and under, around, between.
The loveless noticed nothing at all.
    Fasting, pilgrimage, and the call
    to prayer, love has drowned them all.

Fasts, the Hajj, the prayer, O mother —
the Beloved came and made me forget them all.

When word of the Beloved reached me,
logic and grammar were all forgotten;
love struck the strings of that One alone.
Fasts, the Hajj, the prayer, O mother —
the Beloved came and made me forget them all.

The moment the Beloved entered my house,
I forgot even the Sharh al-Wiqaya;
in every manifestation He alone appears,
His radiance within and without.
The heedless folk have no inkling of it.
Fasts, the Hajj, the prayer, O mother —
the Beloved came and made me forget them all.

translations.text:
All cotton-bolls are white.

Warp and woof, spindle and reel,
back and front, head and heel,
will end up in the one cloth
that will not last the night.

    All cotton-bolls are white.

Khaddar and muslin, coarse or fine,
dress for ploughman, groom, divine,
issue from the self-same loom
no matter what the guise.

    All cotton-bolls are white.

The bangles worn by girls, and rings
and bracelets and such adornings
are from the same silver beaten,
though hands are dark or light.

All cotton-bolls are white.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.107. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training. Rafat compresses the long Punjabi catalogues of loom-parts and cloths into representative pairs._

All are of one colour — all of them cotton.

Warp-thread and warp-beam, weft and spools,
the back-beam, the reed, the shuttle, the rings —
each announces a name of its own,
each goes about under a separate name;
all are of one colour — all of them cotton.

Chunni and fine weave, khaddar and dhoti-cloth,
muslin and khaasa — all a single thread;
each comes forth from the very same spool,
even the saffron robe of the ascetic.
All are of one colour — all of them cotton.

Bangles, arm-rings, signet-rings and bands,
each of them with a name of its own —
call it all one and the same silver:
the kangan, the churra on the arms —
all are of one colour — all of them cotton.

translations.text:
A hundred merchants are here who tell
of rubies they have brought to sell.

Hearing them, I craved immediately
two for my ears so people could see.

Look at my foolishness, I who am
nothing, went off to buy a gem.

What was the price they asked? I cried
at pin-pricks, and they wanted my head.

The lowly should not reach for the sky.
A glass-bead is all they can buy.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.109. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training. Rafat's closing couplet ("The lowly should not reach for the sky…") is a free divergence from the Punjabi ("those who buy rubies must give their heads")._

The traders have come, O mother — the traders have come!
They deal in rubies, crying their wares aloud.

Hearing the cry, my heart was seized: I too will bring home rubies;
I'll set one or two in my ears and show them off to the world.

Raw and untried, I know nothing of trade, yet I set out to buy rubies;
no money in my purse, no credit at all — look, my necklace won't even cover it.

When I asked them the price, they named a heavy one;
I who had never so much as borne a needle's prick — and they demand my very head.

Those who would trade in rubies must first have their heads struck off.
The traders have come, O mother — the traders have come!

translations.text:
Love comes on bright new wings.

I read love's book. Ever since,
mosques have made me wince.
Now I revel in precincts
echoing to a thousand strings.

    Love comes on bright new wings.

Genuflexions night and day
have worn the knee-caps away.
God's not in Tirath or Mecca,
but in hearts where true love sings.

    Love comes on bright new wings.

Scatter the rosary, spurn
ablutions and the prayer-mat burn,
for lovers they sigh and yearn
to taste prohibited things.

    Love comes on bright new wings.

Ranjha is one with his bride.
She looked for him far and wide,
but he had never left her side.
Knowing this, we know all things.

    Love comes on bright new wings.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), pp.111+113. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training. Rafat softens the antinomian line ("eat the forbidden") into "to taste prohibited things."_

Love's spring is forever new.

The moment I read the lesson of love,
my heart shrank away from the mosque;
asking my way, I entered the temple
where a thousand strains resound.
Love's spring is forever new.

Weary from poring over Vedas and Qur'ans,
foreheads worn thin with prostration —
God is neither in Tirath nor in Mecca;
whoever found Him found the Light of lights.
Love's spring is forever new.

Burn the prayer-mat, smash and toss the ablution-pot;
tell no rosary, drop the beggar's staff —
the lovers cry aloud their call:
"Renounce the lawful — eat the forbidden!"
Love's spring is forever new.

Heer and Ranjha have become one;
the bewildered Heer scoured the wild pastures,
while Ranjha, her love, was in her own arms all along.
No awareness stayed — so guard your awareness!
Love's spring is forever new.

translations.text:
Enough of learning, friend.
One A can begin and end.

You study night and day
while life is ticking away,
when all you need is an A.
Enough of learning, friend,
    enough of learning!

The books you read and write
reach up to such a height
they've quite shut off the light.
You know not where you wend,
    enough of learning, friend.

The muezzin shatters the air
while you heap prayer on prayer
and sermons drip from your hair,
but to what end?
    Enough of learning, friend.

Has this knowledge brought relief
or added grief to grief?
You nab the just, and the thief
you fail to apprehend.
    Enough of learning, friend.

Such learning fools elevates
and some fresh bother creates,
is used to con illiterates,
make vows with false intent,
    enough of learning, friend.

Mullahs mug their way to power,
and now are judge and juror;
and avarice grows by the hour,
and straight to hell you wend.
    Enough of learning, friend.

You dream up problems in a wink,
schism is your meat and drink,
beneath saintly garb you stink,
saying what you don't intend,
    enough of learning, friend.

When the bait of Love I cast,
slippery Truth was hooked at last,
and the griefs which held me fast
God's mercy made an end.
    Enough of learning, friend!

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), pp.115+117+119. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training. Rafat renders "Ikko Alif tere darkaar" as "One A can begin and end" and turns the murshid's name (Shah Inayat) into "God's mercy."_

Enough of learning, friend!
A single Alif is all you need.
Learning does not enter the reckoning;
your life slips away — there is no trusting it.
A single Alif is all you need.
Enough of learning, friend!

Reading and writing, you pile up heaps,
heaps of books all around you;
ignorance encircles you, darkness is within;
ask "the way" — and you have not the least news of it.
Enough of learning, friend!

You offer prayer upon voluntary prayer,
cry the call aloud, shout it high,
climb the pulpit and thunder sermons —
learning has only disgraced you.
Enough of learning, friend!

From learning, only more quarrels arise;
those with eyes are blind and sightless;
they seize the holy man and let the thief go free.
Enough of learning, friend!

Reading, reading, you style yourself Shaikh and elder,
you fabricate rulings upside-down,
you plunder the unlettered and devour them,
swearing the false and the true alike.
Enough of learning, friend!

Reading, reading, mullahs become qazis;
God is well pleased even without such learning.
Greed grows fresher by the day —
greed has disgraced you.
Enough of learning, friend!

Reading, reading, you keep reciting rulings,
you feed on the food of doubt and suspicion;
you say one thing and earn by another —
false within, upright without.
Enough of learning, friend!

When I read the lesson of love,
I beheld the river of oneness and plunged in;
I was caught fast in its whirlpools —
[my master] Shah Inayat carried me across!
Enough of learning, friend!

Stop the spinning-wheel, girl.
Gather the cloth, take off the reel, girl.
    Your wedding day
    is just a week away,
    yet you sing and play
    within a shell soon to be peeled, girl.
Stop the spinning-wheel, girl.
    If dowryless you leave
    how can you hope to please?
    Your spouse will grumble and grieve.
    Take heed from one who knows the deal, girl.
Stop the spinning-wheel, girl.

Spin, girl — there will be no next time, girl.
Take the reel off, gather it up now, girl.
Your parents have settled the match;
your senses have not yet come to you;
the days are few, then the farewell —
you will not come to your mother's house again, girl.
Spin, girl — there will be no next time, girl.

If you go without a dowry,
you will please no one at all;
how then will you win over the Beloved?
Grasp the counsel of the faqirs, girl.
Spin, girl — there will be no next time, girl.

Dogs are above you.

You keep vigil at night, performing your worship;
dogs keep awake at night too — they are above you.

They never once leave off their barking,
then go and sleep on the rubbish-heap: above you.

They will not abandon their master's door,
though they be beaten with shoes: above you.

Bulleh Shah! trade for some worthy merchandise,
or else the dogs have won the game — they are above you.

translations.text:
Come see me once in a while.

You are gone, friend, far away
beyond my reach. Many a day
Kasur has missed your smile.
    Come see me once in while.

Now hell has opened its bogs.
Punjab has gone to the dogs.
This hell is the nethermost hell.
    Come see me once in a while.

A brief visit now and then
will give some ease to my pain.
This century cramps our style.
    Come see me once in a while.

The flames engulfing my house,
Bulleh, only love can douse.
Inayat calls up the aisle
    Come see me once in a while.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.129. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training. Rafat keeps "Kasur" and "Inayat" but generalises "the twelfth century" to "This century cramps our style."_

Come, meet me sometime, beloved friend.

You have gone far, far away from us,
and settled somewhere beyond my reach;
why have you forgotten Kasur?
Come, meet me sometime, beloved friend.

The door of doomsday-torment has swung open,
Punjab has fallen into a wretched state;
within these halls a hell now burns.
Come, meet me sometime, beloved friend.

Come to me at least sometime, O kinsman —
the griefs of your absence have slain me;
the twelfth century has bared its ugly face.
Come, meet me sometime, beloved friend.

Bulleh — the Beloved will surely come to my house
and quench the fire that blazes within me.
With every breath I call Inayat to mind.
Come, meet me sometime, beloved friend.

translations.text:
Lass, look to your spinning.

Mother scolds you every day,
but your mind is far away;
you keep modesty at bay;
when will you understand?
    Lass, look to your spinning.

So much advice I hurl
each day at this silly girl;
she will be in a whirl
when bad times are at hand.
    Lass, look to your spinning.

The new cotton crop is in.
Take it for scouring, and then
sit down to spin and spin,
or spinning time will be gone.
    Lass, look to your spinning.

Here you do not belong,
so now switch off this song,
or you will lose the chance
to set up house on your own.
    Lass, look to your spinning.

What you get under this roof
topped with a fond mother's love,
will be lost soon enough.
A tough mother-in-law waits.
    Lass, look to your spinning.

The sun is high. Attend
to your chores, and send
the dowry to the dyer, then
you'll have earned each one's respect.
    Lass, look to your spinning.

You think that you are fair,
take pride in your silken hair,
but who will heed it there?
These will be gone in a trice.
    Lass, look to your spinning.

A time is coming soon
when you'll be left alone,
then help there will be none
till you call on Bulleh's guide.
    Lass, look to your spinning.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), pp.131+133+135. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training. Rafat renders "Bulhe da Sultan" (the murshid/king) as "Bulleh's guide."_

What does this mad lover do? you ask.
He shuttles between temple and mosque.

He is one, but one among many because
there are no secrets in a crowded house.

Everywhere he is seen, each place his own,
for in the stream of oneness none may drown.

Bulleh, love devours all, takes all to task.
What does this mad lover do? you ask.

title: Kaisi tauba (Penitence)

original.text:
کیسی توبہ

کیسی توبہ ہے ایہ توبہ، ایسی توبہ نہ کر یار

مُونہوں توبہ، دِلوں نہ کردا، اِس توبہ تھِیں ترک نہ پھڑدا
کِس غفلت نے پایو پردا، تینوں بخشے کیوں غفار

سانوِیں دے کے لَؤں سوائے، ڈُہڑیاں اُتّے بازی لائے
مُسلمانی اوہ کِتّھوں پائے، جس دا ہووے ایہ کِردار

جِت نہ جانا اُتّے جاویں، حتیٰ بیگانہ ٹھمکر کھاویں
ٹھوڑ کِتاباں سِر تے چاویں، ہووے کِہ تیرا اعتبار

ظالِم ظُلموں ناہیں ڈردے، اپنی کیتیوں آپے مردے
ناہیں خوف خُدا دا کردے، ایتّے اُتّے ہوون خوار

translations.text:
What sort of penitence is this?

That sits on the lips, but has no place in the heart,
and yet expects to be granted bliss;

whose name is Muslim, but whose furtive eyes
look for lacunas; whose ambitions hiss;

whose heart is absent when the hand is placed
on the Holy Book in solemn promise.

O ruthless ones, the trap you set for others,
is set for you. Be sure it will not miss.

What sort of penitence is this?

translations.text:
Who choose cold-hearted dears
must learn to cope with tears.

	Now he is gone
	heart from body is drawn,
	in its place is a stone.
	To advice you turned deaf ears.
		Who choose cold-hearted dears.

	You trust, you fool,
	one with no pity at all,
	who laughs when sparrows fall,
	and claps his hands and jeers.
		Who coose cold-hearted dears.

	He has betrayed
	every promise he made,
	but I still wait and wait,
	undeterred by his sneers.

Who choose cold-hearted dears
must learn to cope with tears.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.141. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

What use is friendship with the pitiless!
My eyes weep, wailing and lamenting.

The heartless one has gone and left me,
having driven the spear of separation into my breast,
having drawn the very life out of my body —
that is the deed he did, unkind friendship.
What use is friendship with the pitiless!

What trust can be placed in the pitiless?
There is not an ounce of fear within his heart.
The sparrows' death is sport to the boorish;
the wretch laughs and claps his hands in glee.
What use is friendship with the pitiless!

He promised to come, then came no more;
he forgot all the vows he made of coming.
I was cheated — I did not deal in deceit —
what a swindling trader I chanced to meet!
What use is friendship with the pitiless!
My eyes weep, wailing and lamenting.

translations.text:
Stop the clock on the wall
for my love has come to call.

	Each swift minute is a bite
	into the span of the night.
	If they knew my plight
	the minute hands would fall.

		My love has come to call.

	Sweet music adds its boon
	to a sweet singer in tune.
	Now prayer and fast are done.
	for the cup is raised in skoal.

		My love has come to call.

	Just one glimpse can fetch
	delight to the meanest wretch.
	To make this short night stretch
	against time throw up a wall.

		My love has come to call.

	To entice him I did use
	all sorts of spells and brews.
	May he, now he's in the house,
	stay a million years in all.

		My love has come to call.

	Bulleh, what is my life
	unless love twists its knife?
	He's come after so much strife
	now may no misfortune befall.

		My love has come to call.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.145. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

Take away the gong, O bell-ringer,
for today my beloved has come home.

Moment by moment he strikes the gong,
lessening the night of union, piya.
If he could grasp what is in my heart
he would fling the gong from his hands.
Take away the gong, O bell-ringer.

The unstruck music sounds so sweetly —
minstrel! strike up the melody and song.
Fasting is forgotten, and the ritual prayers;
the vintner offers the cup of the Faith.
Take away the gong, O bell-ringer.

All my sorrow and want have lifted away;
gazing on his face is a wondrous sight.
The night has grown long — make it stretch out more,
raise a wall against the coming of day.
Take away the gong, O bell-ringer.

I wove endless charms to break the fast of parting;
the great elders came deaf to my plea.
So at last my darling has come to my home —
may the night with him last a hundred thousand years.
Take away the gong, O bell-ringer.

Bulleh, the true love of the Lord is dear;
I am ferried across by the Ferryman.
By small coins my turn has come round at last —
now parting has become impossible.
Take away the gong, O bell-ringer,
for today my beloved has come home.

translations.text:
Up with your veil, love,
and look at me.

	I'm immune to the smears
	on my character. My dear,
	the harder they jeer
	the louder my ecstasy.

		Up with your veil, love,
		and look at me.

	Let my prayer be heard.
	Love, say a word.
	How can a bird
	be blithe sans its tree?

		Up with your veil, love,
		and look at me.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.149. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

Do not hide behind the veil, beloved;
I am longing for the sight of you!

Without you I have become a mad woman,
the whole world of people makes me an outcast.
When I try, my love, to win your favour,
then I raise up my complaint and cry.
Do not hide behind the veil, beloved;
I am longing for the sight of you!

Cheaply the silver bondmaid is sold off;
joined to her beloved she leaves needless things behind.
Not for a single breath can I bear the parting —
I am the nightingale of the flower-garden.
Do not hide behind the veil, beloved;
I am longing for the sight of you!

translations.text:
The horse is clay, and so is the rider —
how strangely clay runs after clay,

	that's its way.

And clay kills clay with a clay sword;
the more clayey one will be the one to slay,

	that's its way.

What's the garden but clay? And its flowers?
Clay has come to it in a season of clay,

	that's its way.

Four elements spin the world, but a fifth
overrules them, while the rest betray;

	that's their way.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.151. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

The clay takes the pace of the beloved.

Clay the saddle, clay the horse, clay the rider,
clay makes clay gallop, clay is the clatter of it.
The clay takes the pace of the beloved!

Clay set out to slay clay, clay the weapon;
whichever clay has the more clay, that clay is proud.
The clay takes the pace of the beloved!

Clay the garden, clay the orchard, clay its rose-bed;
clay came to gaze on clay, clay is the springtime of it.
The clay takes the pace of the beloved!

Four elements joined together to play,
and in the fifth is the chieftain;
having laughed and played, they turn back to clay,
falling and stretching out their feet.
The clay takes the pace of the beloved!

I'm harbouring a thief.
Since he wears my guise how can I give him away?
If he tiptoes out there will be hell to pay.
        I'm harbouring a thief.

Some will understand, others will scratch their head.
Will the pother end if he's not the one they expect?
        I'm harbouring a thief.

The rulers of Lahore under threatening skies
put their hands to their ears and shut their eyes.
        I'm harbouring a thief.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.155. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

There is a thief tucked in the fold of my shawl!

Within the fold of my shawl is a theft; within my shawl there is a thief.

Friends, to whom shall I cry out and tell: there is a thief in the fold of my shawl.
Stealthily he slipped away, and an uproar broke out in the world.
        A thief in the fold of my shawl.

Whoever recognized him understood the secret, while the others kept up their whirling dance and clamour.
All the quarrels and squabbles wore themselves out — some other one had slipped away.
        A thief in the fold of my shawl.

From the heavens the call to prayer was answered, the throne of Lahore heard it.
Shah Inayat has tied the knots; grown weary, he keeps his silence far off.
        Within the fold of my shawl is a theft; within my shawl there is a thief.

چنگے چنگیرے پکڑ منگاسے، مَیں کمَیدی پہلائی
جِس گُنّی پلّے بول سَوتّے، سوئی ہووے نوں پیاری

translations.text:
Gather round me, friends, my stay here is done.
I'm off to the house where you'll join me soon.

What was my dowry?  A stove and a shawl.
When I think of it now the tear-drops fall.
Like a lost crane I'll roam when I leave you all.

So many arrows of pain that struck home
deck the body, but what of those to come?
They will sneer at me there; this is my doom.

All must go, of remission not a word.
Who am I, when my betters were not spared?
Only the righteous will get bed and board.

Gather round me, friends, my stay here is done.
I'm off to the house where you'll join me soon.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.157. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

Come, meet me, dear companions

Come and meet me, my beloved friends, my playmates — I am going to my in-laws' house.
This will be God's will for you too; I am going to my in-laws' house.
The dowry my mother and father gave me: one bodice, one veil.
Seeing the dowry others were given, my heart is filled to the brim.
One is the parting of stitched seams — like a crane cut off from her flock.

My own pains, of many colours, tear at and rend my soul.
By the sorrow of this place I am forewarned — to whom shall I make the next vows?
The cheap and worthless ones cast their taunts; a great shame falls on me.

Here we are not granted to stay; each in turn must go.
They will seize and demand the best of the best; I am the least-worthy one.
Whichever bride carries sweet words in her lap, she alone is dear.
Come and meet me, my beloved friends, my playmates — I am going to my in-laws' house.
This will be God's will for you too; I am going to my in-laws' house.

translations.text:
Truth will out

        though it adds fuel to fire.
        Lies are a burnt-out pyre.
        So after looking at both
                the tongue must shout,
                truth will out.

        In the darkness walk with care
        for floors are slippery here.
        Ascertain who is within
                while others hunt without.
                Truth will out.

        Who knows what the sadhu knows
        will surely find repose.
        On the tideless river of peace
                he is afloat.
                Truth will out.

        Whatever the time and place
        God is in every face.
        Unalterable this fact
                covert or not.
                Truth will out.

        The lessons experience taught
        have all been dearly bought.
        The rest is a stream's babble
                not worth a thought.
                Truth will out.

        Love, Bulleh, is part of us
        without which is nothing but fuss.
        If only we had the eyes
                we would not doubt.
                Truth will out.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.159–161. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

The word that rises to the lips will not stay unspoken

If I speak the truth, a blaze flares up;
if I tell a lie, nothing is saved.
The heart weighs both these matters —
truth speaks out just as truth is.
The word that rises to the lips will not stay unspoken.

This is a slippery playing-field, a courtyard;
tread step by step, for it is dark.
Look which one is the bridegroom within —
why does creation go searching outside?
The word that rises to the lips will not stay unspoken.

Whoever has grasped the secret of the qalandar,
who has sought the path within himself,
he is a dweller in the temple of bliss,
a place where none rises and none sets.
The word that rises to the lips will not stay unspoken.

One condition is binding — the courtesy of restraint;
to us the matter of all is known.
In each and every one is the face of the Lord,
somewhere manifest, somewhere hidden.
The word that rises to the lips will not stay unspoken.

We have studied the science of inquiry —
there is but one true letter there;
all the rest of the wrangling is excess,
people just sit raising a needless din.
The word that rises to the lips will not stay unspoken.

O my Beloved, Bulleh! Away from you there is no grief that is grief;
without the Beloved there is no other joy.
But there is no eye that truly sees,
and so the soul endures its separations.
The word that rises to the lips will not stay unspoken.

God has come down as man.

        He is deer and leopard, kills and is killed,
        he is master and slave, sells and is sold.

God has come down as man.

        I am a puppet on a string, and such
        is his control, I tremble at a touch.

God has come down as man.

The Lord has become man.

The Lord has become man.

He himself is the deer, himself the leopard, himself the one who springs to kill;
himself the master, himself the slave, himself sold at a price.
The Lord has become man.

What a game the juggler has played — he has made me dance like a puppet.
I dance to whatever measure the Friend has taught and written for me.
The Lord has become man.

translations.text:
I'm waiting, pass this way once more,
Inayat Shah, my eyes are sore
with looking for you at the door.

        I'm waiting, pass this way once more.

Who will lead me to the place
of my master, so by his grace
he may my heart and body restore.

        I'm waiting, pass this way once more.

See, I am dressed to the nines
for that cold man.  I see no signs
of him, and am stricken to the core.

        I'm waiting, pass this way once more.

Bulleh, every beat of your heart
cries love, but the tears start
to the eyes when they see what's in store.

        I'm waiting, pass this way once more.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.165. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

I keep on waiting

I keep on waiting — come round, pass this way once more.
I have spread the bed at dusk, my heart has grown desolate.
Where have you hidden yourself — come, my Shah Inayat.
I keep on waiting — come round, pass this way once more.

Who is there of a kind to go and speak my word,
what fault is in me, I who am your slave?
Apart from you who is mine — my heart is breaking.
I keep on waiting — come round, pass this way once more.

Bangles on my wrist, glass bracelets on my arm, a bright-coloured tunic at my throat;
some beloved has raised a great clamour in me.
Swaying, I sink down again and again — your heart is stone.
I keep on waiting — come round, pass this way once more.

O Bulleh! for the Beloved's sake the heart blazes and burns;
hard is the road of love, the pain never lessens.
The quarrel throbs within my heart — I bow my head.
I keep on waiting — come round, pass this way once more.

translations.text:
I'm just a sweepress.

Hair uncombed, barefoot, I receive word
of his coming, and am left perturbed.
The broom my meditation: with it I've swept
into my basket all that the world has kept.
The judge knows much, the king rules with fear,
but I'm happy to be allowed in here.

I'm just a sweepress.

Being untouchable, none comes near
me, but I'm on the way, I do not care.
What's my pay after a hard day's grind?
A hard pillow, and what you leave behind.
This is my life: cold and sickness and scorn;
an empty stomach, clothes that are torn.
The straws of my broom are all that I own.

I'm just a sweepress.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.167. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

I am but a sweepress at the court of the true Lord.
Barefoot, my head loosely wrapped, word has reached me from afar.
I have broken all bonds — I am no one now — what shall I take from the world?
My reflection is the small broom, my knowledge the sweeper: daily I sweep away lust and rage.
I catch hold of lightning, I drive off greed, I answer to the tax-collectors.
The qazi knows, the ruler knows — I am done with forced, unpaid labour.
Night and day this alone I beg: do not turn me away from your court.
I am but a sweepress at the court of the true Lord.

What of the sweeper-woman, what of her low caste — everyone spurns us.
Having done drudgery and unpaid toil, in the end one must go to the Master.
What wages are read out for the sweeper-woman? A knot of cloth and a hard pillow.
Whatever the Master himself has given, that alone one carries home.
Our lot is a worn-out rag — hunger, a dry crust: this is the truth, this our fate.
Starving and famished, begging and pleading — such is our way of life.
[Uncertain line] — coarse straws and reeds, these are our trade.
I am but a sweepress at the court of the true Lord.

translations.text:
What I've picked up costs me dear.

Its thorns are sharp, my clothes are torn,
I must deal with one cold to the bone,
his servants tax each stick I own
which is quite a bundle.  As soon
as it is tied, the merchants will be here.

What I've picked up costs me dear.

The slope is steep, and heavy the load
on my head, and I stumble on the road.
My misspent life tells on my face,
I am so weak and lacking in grace,
not Bulleh, but Inayat must steer.

What I've picked up costs me dear.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.169. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

I have picked the safflowers one by one — and lost.

The thorns of this safflower-bush are cruel: flying about, my veil is torn.
The overseer of this bush is harsh, and the record-keeper is a tyrant.
This bush has four headmen who demand a heavy levy.
For others I gathered blossom by blossom, and filled up my basket-cloth.
Whatever I picked and heaped up, the merchants carry off.

The pass is hard, the road is difficult, and the bundle on my head is heavy.
The virtuous ones have all crossed over; only I, the sinner, am left behind.
I have thrown away my whole life at play, and lost the game at the last throw.
I am low-born, loud, ill-favoured, without merit — a wretched thing.
Bulleh is not worthy of the Beloved; Shah Inayat, ferry me across.
I have picked the safflowers one by one — and lost.

From the first moment love
has put me to the proof.

He tossed me in the frying-pan,
and tosses me over again.

Not satisfied with my death,
he kills with every breath.

One ember on the body
spread till it engulfed me.

Bulleh, love will not settle
for less, your most is little.

From the first moment love
has put me to the proof.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.171. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

Love has seized me — a strange, first love,
love from the beginning, from the day of eternity.

It throws me into the cauldron bit by bit,
frying the sesame-seeds one by one.

Again and again it strikes down the already-slain,
grinding the hearts to a pulp.

How should I know? Some friend must have learned this game —
a thorn forever pierces my breast.

Bulleh! the Beloved's love is a wondrous thing;
He does not mingle with just anyone who tries.
Love has seized me — a strange, first love,
love from the beginning, from the day of eternity.

translations.text:
Strange are the ways of my love!

To sleep I have kissed goodbye;
on the roof I mope and sigh
while mirages green my eye.
No peace in city or grove.

To glimpse is to die. One look
and the noose is round your neck.
I should have kept it in check,
but Lahore's thug covered his bluff.

Strange are the ways of my love!

Lovers walk silently where
is nobody else, and they stare
through the bars of silken hair,
strength from their limbs drained off.

Bulleh, what can you hope to find
when love is totally blind?
It is just a state of mind
that knows nor smooth nor rough.

Strange are the ways of my love!

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), pp.173, 175. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

How wonderful — the mystery of the Beloved is something else!

I climb onto the rooftop and call out:
is there anyone who deals in love?
Its price is nothing less than swallowing deceit,
yet neither in the wild nor in the town is it even spoken of.

The instant of the vision led me astray;
all at once the matter fell upon me from behind.
It played a fierce indifference with me —
the thug of Lahore is the one I met.
How wonderful — the mystery of the Beloved is something else!

The lovers move about hushed and silent,
as if forever drunk, intoxicated with wine,
caught fast in the snare of the beloved's tresses —
there no strength or force will avail.

Bulleh! the Beloved's love is a wondrous thing:
whoever has seen it does not count it up.
It has no colour, no form, no outline —
he alone becomes it who first becomes its thief.
How wonderful — the mystery of the Beloved is something else!

Neither Hindu nor Muslim
I sit with all on a whim.
Having no caste, sect, or creed,
I am different indeed.
Neither thirsty nor quite slaked,
I am not dressed nor naked.
I do not laugh, do not cry,
and neither stay nor go by.
I am not sinner or saint
knowing nor sin nor restraint.
Bulleh tries hard to shirk
the embrace of Hindu and Turk.

Neither Hindu nor Muslim — I sit apart from all, casting off pride.
Not a Sunni, nor are we a Shia: I have taken the road of peace-with-all.
Not hungry, nor are we sated; not naked, nor are we clothed.
Not weeping, nor are we laughing; not ruined, nor are we settled.
Not a sinner, nor called righteous — I do not know the way of sin or merit.

Bulleh Shah! whoever fixes the heart on the Lord
casts off both beings — Turk and Hindu alike.

جدوں اَحد اِک اِکلا سی، نہ ظاہر کوئی تجلا سی
نہ رب رسول نہ اللہ سی، نہ سی جبار تے نہ قہار

بے چُون و بے چگُون سی، بے شبہے تے بے نمونہ سی
نہ کوئی رنگ نمونہ سی، ہُن ہویا گوناگُون ہزار

پھیر کُن کیہا فیکون کمایا، بے چُونی توں چُون بنایا
احد دے وچ میم رلایا، تاہیوں کیتا احمد پیار

ہُن میں لکھیا سوہنا یار، جس دے حُسن دا گرم بازار

پیر پیغمبر اُس دے بردے، اِنس ملائک سجدے کردے
سر قدماں دے اُتے دھردے، سب توں وڈی اوہ سرکار

تجوں مسیت تجوں بُت خانہ، برتی رہاں نہ روزہ جاناں
بھُلا وضو، نماز دوگانہ، تینیں پر جان کراں نثار

جو کوئی اُس نوں لکھیا چاہے، بے وسیلے نہ لکھیا جائے
شاہ عنایت بھیت بتائے، تاہیں کھُلے سب اسرار

translations.text:
I've tracked the beauty down
which was the talk of the town.

    A Word existed in space
    which had no form or face.
    None mighty or small.
    No God or prophet at all.

I've tracked the beauty down
which was the talk of the town.

    The Word had no sire or heir,
    it was beyond compare.
    It had no colour or smell.
    There was no heaven or hell.

I've tracked the beauty down
which was the talk of the town.

    Then the Word was mated
    and angels and saints created
    to choir around His seat,
    and kneel at His feet.

I've tracked the beauty down
which was the talk of the town.

    And God was temple and mosque
    and all you could ask,
    but cold to fast and prayer-call.
    He was above them all.

I've tracked the beauty down
which was the talk of the town.

    Only the proper guide
    can lead you to His side;
    and unless you choose
    Inayat, you will lose.

I've tracked the beauty down
which was the talk of the town.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), pp.183, 185. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

Now I have written down the beautiful Beloved, whose beauty holds a hot market [is in great demand].

When the One (aḥad) was alone, single — no manifest radiance shone forth,
there was no Lord, no Messenger, no Allah; neither the Almighty nor the Wrathful was yet.

Without quality and without likeness He was, without doubt and without pattern;
no colour or model was there — now He has become a thousandfold, of every hue.

Then He spoke "Be!" and made "it becomes" (kun fayakūn), out of the quality-less He fashioned quality;
into the "one" (aḥad) He mingled a "mīm" — and so He loved [it as] "Aḥmad."

Now I have written down the beautiful Beloved, whose beauty holds a hot market.

Saints and prophets are His slaves; men and angels bow in prostration,
they lay their heads upon His feet — He is the highest court of all.

For Him I would forsake the mosque, forsake the idol-temple; I keep no fast, know no ritual observance,
forget ablution and the two-cycle prayer — upon You I would offer up my very life.

Whoever would seek to write [know] Him, cannot write [reach] Him without a means [a guide];
let Shāh ʿInāyat reveal the secret, and then all mysteries are opened.

translations.text:
You came and I had to fall.
But why did you come at all?

    Abraham set alight,
    Zachariah sawn in half,
    Joseph was auctioned off.
    And what will be my lot?

        You came and I had to fall.
        But why did you come at all?

    Sanaan made to feed swine,
    Shams was skinned alive,
    Mansur crucified.
    Now I must toe the line.

You came and I had to fall.
But why did you come at all?

    Whatever house you tried
    was burnt to the ground;
    on the ash-heap you were found.
    Are you now satisfied?

        You came and I had to fall.
        But why did you come at all?

    Bulleh, do what you're told:
    turn your body to a stove
    for the forging of love.
    A red-hot rod now hold.

        You came and I had to fall.
        But why did you come at all?

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), pp.187 & 189. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

Why has love descended upon us?
You came, and I was caught [undone].

Abraham was set upon the pyre;
Zakariya's head was laid to the saw;
Yusuf was sold off, shop to shop —
say then, what has [this love] taken from us?

Why has love descended upon us?
You came, and I was caught.

Shaikh Sanʿan was set to herd swine;
Shams was flayed, his skin peeled off;
Mansur was raised upon the gallows —
so lay your hand [take heart]: on whom now has the heart been set?

Why has love descended upon us?
You came, and I was caught.

Whatever house you turned toward
burned down to a heap of coals;
and when the ash blew away, it was leveled —
say then, on what account has your servant been laid low?

Why has love descended upon us?
You came, and I was caught.

Sit down for the sake of the Beloved:
make your body the furnace, your heart the anvil;
strike the hammer of love within,
until the iron is beaten soft — on whom has [your heart] snagged?

Why has love descended upon us?
You came, and I was caught.

translations.text:
I told the spirits to go
and I would quickly follow,
but I threw up a screen, so
I would not stand out clear.

     I'm not talking of here,
     that's why I quake with fear.

This world has bound me fast;
even if I'm first, I'm last.
What use are these assets, alas,
my balance-sheet is up there.

     I'm not talking of here,
     that's why I quake with fear.

When robbed I shook with grief
and ran hard after the thief,
and found a clue. Now I've
made plundering my career.

     I'm not talking of here,
     that's why I quake with fear.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.193. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

I am speaking of that other place!

I made a promise with the spirits:
"You go ahead — I've come right behind you."
But here I hung a curtain of silence,
and, lost in illusion, still I wander.
I am speaking of that other place,
yet even to speak of it, I am afraid.

My game is played against the whole world;
if I say "mine," even that is torn from me.
The capital laid up and gathered — it is his;
I must yet settle the account that lies ahead.
I am speaking of that other place,
yet even to speak of it, I am afraid.

Handing over my capital, the fool grew flustered,
and set off in pursuit behind the thieves,
and I myself brought back the thieves' own track —
every night now I mount another raid.
I am speaking of that other place,
yet even to speak of it, I am afraid.

are the piercing arrows of love.

translations.text:
Take me, love, under your care;
my woes are too much to bear.

     This troubled heart lacks grace
     and laughs in my face.
     When I ask a question
     it takes like a hawk to the air.

          Take me, love, under your care;
          my woes are too much to bear.

     Love is a raging river
     in whose tumult I quiver
     and which sucks me under,
     while dark clouds shake their hair.

          Take me love, under your care:
          my woes are too much to bear.

     In the basket you tote
     pains writhe. A coiled rope
     gleams like a snake.
     None can escape your snare.

          Take me, love, under your care;
          my woes are too much to bear.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.201. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

You take charge of my affair.

Take charge of my affair —
some heavy debt has fallen due.

This heart that dwells within me
sits beside me and laughs at me;
when I ask it questions, it starts up and flies off,
soaring away like a hawk.
You take charge of my affair.

Now I have plunged into the deep rivers,
come face to face with the surging waves;
the whirlpools have seized and spun me round,
and overhead the rain, the dark of night.
You take charge of my affair.

What swings have you set me on?
You hid the stars in a basket;
you turned the rope of rushes into a serpent.
I am a sacrifice to your wedding-crowns.
You take charge of my affair.

Saturday — restless — see, by my beloved's oath,
I shall not turn homeward again; what has been will be.

Ah, Saturday, the idle hours:
the pain of my beloved has turned me sallow.
I search the wilderness, the forest, the wilds;
the night has strayed, the moments have twisted about me —
the pangs of separation encircle me.

Every hour, every blink, longings assail me.
Nights, sweet crossings-over now gone by;
I climb high and cry out, I shout aloud,
splinters of parting rasp within my breast —
these longings, beloved, are for you.

Thursday is lovely — no grief, no pain, no sin was there:

تُھور تُھور عِنایت وَستے پیہا کرے پُکار

سوہن ملھاراں سارے ساوَن
دُوتی دُکھ لگّے اُٹھ جاوَن
بِنینگر کھیڈن، گڈیاں گاوَن
مَیں گھر رنگ رنگیلے آوَن
آساں پُنّیاں

میریاں آساں رَبّ پُچّائیاں
سِتیاں دین مُبارک آئیاں
مَیں تاں اُن سنگ اکھیاں لائیاں
شاہ عِنایت رنگ لگائیاں
آساں پُنّیاں

translations.text:
RAIN

Rain on time brings joy to all
is what the koels call.

          Sweet sounds the flute,
          boys and girls are at play,
          now my sighs bear fruit,
          love has come to stay.

                    Barriers fall.

          Friends hurry to my side
          with 'Lucky, lucky you.'
          My mentor, my guide
          made my dreams come true.

                    Love is all.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), p.209. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

Rain

Lovely is the rain-season, the clouds and the drizzle; the thunder-cloud is fair as it gathers,
and drop by drop the grace pours down — the pied cuckoo cries out for it.

Beautiful are the malhaar songs all through the rains;
the sorrow that once made me rise and leave has fled.
Girl-companions play, they sing at their spinning-wheels,
and to my house the many-hued colours have come —
my hopes are fulfilled.

God has heard my prayers;
my friends have come with the blessings of the faith.
As for me, I fixed my eyes upon Him:
Shah Inayat has coloured me with his hue —
my hopes are fulfilled.

title: Keho surti gal kaaj di main gundhaan ketiaan paawaan (Knots)

original.text:
گنڈھاں

کیہو سُرتی گل کاج دی مَیں گنڈھاں کیتیاں پاواں
ساہے تے وِیج آوَسی، تُہن چاہلی گنڈھ گھتاواں
بابل آکھیا آن کے، تَیں ساہوریاں گھر جانا
رِیت اوتھوں دی اورَ ہَے، مُڑ پَیر نہ ایتھے پانا
گنڈھ پہلی نوں کھول کے، مَیں بَیٹھی بِرلاواں
اوڑک جاوَن جاوَتاں، تُہن مَیں داج رنگاواں
دیکھوں طرف بزار دی، سب رِستے لاگے
پلّے کُجھ نہ روکڑی، سب مُجھ سے بھاگے

کر بسم اللہ کھولیاں، مَیں گنڈھاں چاہلی
جس اپنا آپ ونجالیا، سو سُرجِن والی
وِیج سوہنی مَیں بھاوَندی، مُکلیندا آوَے
جس نوں عِشق ہَے لال دا، سو لال ہو جاوَے
عقل فِکر سب چھوڑ کے، شوہ نال سدھاوَے
گنڈھوں بِن، گل غیب دی اَساں یاد نہ کائے
تُہن اِنّا للہ آکھ کے، تُم کرو نِگاہیں
اللہ ہی سب ہو گیا، عبد اللہ نا ہیں

translations.text:
KNOTS

How many knots shall I tie,
                    dear, tell me true?
Forty days to the wedding,
                    so forty will do.
Father has told me I must
                    go to the bourne
of my in-laws, from which
                    none shall return.
The first knot I opened, and
                    grumbled and cried,
should the dresses be sequinned,
                    or should they be dyed?
I went off to the market with
                    an empty purse,
and the merchants supplied me
                    a push and a curse.

At last when the fortieth
                    knot was undone,
those who had finished their chores
                    was nary a one.
The loud procession is here,
                    this is the day
when the ready and the unready will
                    be taken away,
to be with the master and
                    sit by his side
remembering nothing at all but
                    she's his bride.
Now the last rites are ended, and
                    the bright room
is empty of guests. No one there
                    but bride and groom.

_Reference translation by Taufiq Rafat, "Bulleh Shah: A Selection" (Vanguard, 1982), pp.211, 213. COPYRIGHTED — private reference only; do NOT publish or use for training._

Knots

What sense have I of the wedding-business — how many knots am I to tie?
The date will come at the fixed hour; let me quickly tie the knots.
Father said, coming to me: you must go to your in-laws' house;
the custom there is otherwise — once gone, you shall never set foot here again.
Undoing the first knot, I sat and wept aloud.
The days of leaving run out at last; now let me have my dowry dyed.
I look toward the marketplace — every relation has set off,
nothing in my pocket, no ready cash; they have all fled from me.

Saying "Bismillah," I began to undo the knots quickly.
Whoever has lost her own self, she is the one who reaches the Beloved.
Lovely is the date; longing, I wait — the one who takes the bride away is coming.
Whoever loves the Beloved becomes the Beloved.
Leaving behind all reason and worry, she sets out with the Bridegroom.
Without untying the knots, we gave no thought to the matter of the Unseen.
Now say "Inna lillah" and cast your gaze:
All has become God alone — there is no servant of God any more.
